name: Rouen
title: Rouen Ship Thickness Measurement | UTM for Grain Carriers
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Rouen on the Seine: bulk carriers, product tankers and coasters, hold and ballast tank gauging, pre-docking UTM readings.
h1: Hull and Hold Gauging for Ships Loading at Rouen on the Seine
intro: Rouen is a river port, reached by a long tidal passage up the Seine, and its grain, fertiliser and petroleum quays keep bulk carriers, product tankers and coasters alongside for days at a time. That time is what thickness gauging needs. Superintendents use a Rouen stay to measure holds, hatch covers and ballast tanks before a ship sails for a docking elsewhere. Atlantis sends technicians from India to join the ship at the quay for each job.

highlights.p: Bulk carriers loading cereals at Rouen spend days on the berth. Holds are cleaned before loading, so the empty hold, its frames and the hatch coamings can be measured in the gap between arrival and the first grab.

highlights.h: Upriver stay before a docking elsewhere
highlights.p: Most large ships leaving Rouen go to a yard on the coast or abroad. Readings taken on the river turn the yard's allowance for steel into a measured list well before the ship reaches the dock.

highlights.h: Quay work with the tide in mind
highlights.p: River passages are timed to the tide and to pilot boarding. The gauging plan is written around the berthing and sailing times the ship's agent confirms, with the most critical spaces measured first.

port.h: Rouen: a deep-sea port that sits well inland
p: Rouen lies a long way up the Seine, roughly a hundred kilometres or more from the open sea by the river's own course, and ships reach it by a tidal passage through the estuary and the meanders below the city. The port is part of HAROPA PORT, the joint authority that also runs Le Havre and the Paris river terminals, and it is the one of the three where deep-sea cargo ships come right into the heart of a city and a major industrial zone. Quays stretch along both banks through the city and the industrial suburbs downstream, so a single call can mean a berth in the middle of town or beside a processing plant.

The trades are those of a farming and industrial hinterland. Rouen is among the main grain export ports in Europe, and the cereal terminals load bulk carriers of many sizes through the harvest months and well beyond. Fertiliser, animal fodder, timber, scrap metal, sugar and other dry bulk move through the quays as well. Petroleum products arrive and leave by product tanker for the river-side storage and the chemical works. Container feeders and general cargo ships call on the quays nearest the city, and passenger ships tie up in the centre of town when the cruise programme brings them upriver.

For inspection, the character of the port is the long, planned stay. A bulk carrier arrives, waits for the grain, loads, and sails on a tide. Between arrival and loading the holds are empty and clean, which is when the structure can be reached properly. Ships waiting for a berth lie at the Seine's lay-by points or downstream near the estuary, giving a second window. The bridges across the lower Seine limit the air draught of the tallest ships, and every transit depends on pilot availability and tide, so a ship's time at the quay is more predictable than its arrival, and the work is sequenced from the moment the ship is made fast.

facilities.h: Where ships can be gauged around Rouen
p: Most gauging at Rouen is done alongside, at the grain terminals and the general cargo quays. A bulk carrier that has discharged or that arrives in ballast presents empty holds, which can be entered once the ship's enclosed-space procedure allows it, and the hold frames, tank top, hatch coamings and cover panels are measured at that point. Ballast tanks are worked in parallel by a second pair of technicians where the schedule requires it. A ship that is already loading cannot be measured in its working holds, so the plan puts hold readings ahead of the first cargo operation and moves to the ballast tanks and deck after that.

Product tankers at the river-side oil and chemical berths are treated according to the terminal's rules. Cargo tanks are not entered while cargo is worked, and instruments on deck need the terminal's permission in hazardous zones, but ballast tanks of a laden ship are accessible and are the usual target. Ships that need a drydock normally leave the river for a yard at Le Havre, on the Channel coast or elsewhere in Europe, though HAROPA lists ship repair among the services of the Seine ports, and minor repair afloat at a river quay is possible. A launch is rarely needed because nearly everything happens at a quay.
list: Grain terminals on the Seine — empty hold, hatch coaming and cover gauging on bulk carriers before the first loading operation.
General cargo and dry-bulk quays downstream of the city — tank top, frames, ballast tanks and deck plating on coasters and multipurpose ships.
River-side petroleum and chemical berths — ballast tank and deck gauging on product tankers within the terminal's safety rules.
City-centre quays — hull and deck checks on passenger ships and small cargo vessels during a scheduled stay.
Seine lay-by and waiting points — readings on ships held for a berth or for the tide, subject to launch and safety arrangements.
Repair quays at the Seine ports — wall-thickness checks on piping and deck structure while minor repair is done afloat.

context.h: Regulation and trade pressures on the Seine
p: Port state control in France is carried out under the Paris MoU by the Centres de sécurité des navires of the French maritime administration, and ships calling at Rouen are inspected under the same risk-based targeting as at the coast. A bulk carrier with corroded hatch coamings, wasted hold frames or defective air pipes is the kind of ship that draws a detailed inspection. Measuring the holds before the ship has been loaded, rather than after an inspector has seen them, lets the master and the superintendent decide what to repair on the river and what to defer to the next dock.

Ships calling at EU ports must also carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, and voyages are subject to EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime requirements. Grain carriers are often mid-life or older, and ships over about fifteen years face broader survey gauging at their third renewal. For bulk carriers the framework is the Enhanced Survey Programme and the IACS requirements for bulk carrier hull surveys, with coamings, hold frames and ballast tanks the areas where substantial corrosion is most often found. Superintendents planning a docking after the Seine call use the readings to prepare the steel estimate for the yard.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Rouen
jobs.p: Jobs at Rouen are shaped by the grain season and the tide. The superintendent sends the class's gauging requirements, the loading plan and any areas known to be wasted, and we organise the team so holds and ballast tanks are measured in the order the berth allows. A cleaned hold on arrival is the best window, so the work often starts within the first hours after the ship is made fast. Typical requests look like this:
list: Hold frame, tank top and coaming gauging on a bulk carrier arriving in ballast, measured before the grain loading begins.
Hatch cover panel and coaming thickness measurement on a ship with a history of weathertightness findings, ahead of a flag or class inspection.
Pre-docking readings on ballast tanks of a mid-life bulk carrier, so the steel renewal list is ready when it reaches its yard.
Ballast tank and deck gauging on a product tanker at a river-side berth, combined with wall-thickness checks on ballast and fire-main piping.
Condition gauging for a buyer's inspector on a coaster or multipurpose ship during a scheduled quay stay.

logistics: Teams normally fly to Paris Charles de Gaulle and reach Rouen by train or road, while the small regional airport near the city is not a practical route from India. The ship's agent arranges port passes for the named technicians at the terminal in question, which differ between the grain, petroleum and city quays. France belongs to the Schengen area, so every technician needs a Schengen visa, and we apply once the call is firm, with an invitation from the owner or agent. Travel is booked against the pilot and tide timetable the agent confirms for the ship.

River cruise and small passenger ships

faqs.q: Can holds on a grain carrier be gauged at Rouen?
faqs.a: Yes, while they are empty. A bulk carrier arriving in ballast or after discharge has clean holds, and frames, tank top and coamings can be measured before loading starts. Once cargo is going in, the working holds are closed to us, so the sequence puts hold gauging first and moves to ballast tanks and deck structure while loading continues.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock at Rouen for a docking survey?
faqs.a: Ships that need a docking normally leave the Seine for a yard at the coast, such as Le Havre, or elsewhere in Europe. Some repair work afloat can be done at river quays. What we offer at Rouen is the gauging beforehand, so the yard specification is written from measured steel instead of an allowance.

faqs.q: How does the tidal river passage affect the schedule?
faqs.a: The passage up and down the Seine is timed to the tide and to pilot boarding, so berthing and sailing times move. We plan around the times the ship's agent confirms and measure the most critical spaces first, so that a delayed arrival or an early sailing costs the least important readings.

faqs.q: Can ballast tanks of a laden product tanker be measured at a river berth?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Ballast tanks are separate from the cargo tanks and are often empty on a laden arrival, so they can be entered with the permits in place while cargo is worked. Instruments on deck in hazardous zones need the terminal's permission, and anything the terminal will not allow is left for a later stop.
